column5: two litigants and a claim to be right
column6: The commentary opens with opposing parties each claiming haqq; the first litigant in this proverb appears right until the other examines him, making mutual testing of claims necessary.
Abram asks Lot to end the quarrel between their herdsmen because they are brothers; it gives a concrete family scene for replacing contention with an acknowledged bond.
The commentary's enemy-to-friend turn takes patient action; the law orders one who meets an enemy's wandering ox or donkey to bring it back to him, acting for an adversary's good.
The commentary's former opponents can stand beside one another; the law orders help for the burdened donkey of someone who hates you, turning estrangement into practical cooperation.
The commentary combines the reversal of enmity with urging food for the poor; this proverb commands giving bread and water to a hungry, thirsty enemy.
The commentary's estranged people become a connected company; this psalm calls brothers dwelling together good and pleasant, giving the restored kinship its communal image.

column5: truthful speech and judgments of peace
column6: The commentary moves haqq from a disputed possession to something exchanged for peace; this verse requires each to speak truth to his neighbor and render judgments that make peace.
The commentary joins truth with the removal of estrangement; this command joins loving truth and peace, rather than using a claim of truth to sustain conflict.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel gives another person what he needs; this law requires reproof of a fellow rather than hidden hatred, so truthful correction serves a continuing relationship.
The commentary replaces mutual grievance with affection; this neighboring law forbids vengeance and grudges against one's people and commands love of neighbor.

column5: those who fear God speak with one another
column6: The commentary stresses the reciprocal verb, each giving and receiving counsel; here the God-fearing speak to one another, and their shared speech is remembered before God.
The commentary makes sabr the way from enmity to closeness; this proverb says a hot-tempered person stirs strife while one slow to anger quiets contention.
The commentary's friendship and kinship can be severed by contest; this proverb names gossip as what separates intimate companions, showing the reverse movement of its counsel.
The commentary's two-sided advising means each helps the other; iron sharpening iron depicts a person's face being sharpened by a friend rather than one-sided instruction.
The commentary's close friend can pass truth to another even when difficult; the proverb calls a friend's wounds faithful, making correction an act of loyalty.
The commentary brings truth and restored affection into one relation; this psalm has steadfast love and faithfulness meeting and righteousness and peace kissing.
The commentary begins in opposed claims and seeks a shared right; this instruction requires judges to hear disputes between brothers and judge rightly, supplying a social practice for adjudication.
The opening disputants both claim haqq; this law places two disputants before judges who vindicate the righteous and condemn the wicked, keeping a verdict distinct from rival assertions.
The commentary depicts reconciliation interrupting fear and separation; this proverb likens the beginning of strife to released water and urges stopping it before a quarrel breaks out.
The commentary reverses the pull of contention; this proverb calls abstaining from strife an honor while a fool breaks into quarrels.
The commentary places good deeds beside shared truth and patience; this verse says the work of righteousness will be peace, making just action the condition of settled relations.
The commentary's right is to circulate between people and is paired with mercy in its parallel Qur'anic formulation; this command joins true judgments to mercy and compassion toward one another.
The commentary cites the failure to urge feeding the poor as failed reciprocity; this verse forbids oppression of widow, orphan, sojourner and poor and forbids plotting evil against one another.

column5: share bread and do not hide from kin
column6: The commentary's poor person needs active care, while affection preserves human bonds; Isaiah commands sharing bread with the hungry and not hiding from one's own flesh.
The commentary's first scene is two sides disputing right despite their possible bond; Paul names the scandal of a brother bringing a brother to court before unbelievers.
The commentary's rival claims need someone to reconcile or judge them; Paul asks whether no wise person in the community can decide a matter between brothers.
The commentary's human being is in loss until a shared ethic replaces contention; Paul calls lawsuits among believers already a defeat and asks why they do not bear wrong.
The commentary turns reciprocal contention into joined counsel; Paul urges the community to agree in speech and be restored to one mind without divisions.
The commentary begins with a community at odds; Paul reports quarrels among the Corinthian brothers, the precise communal fracture addressed by his appeal to unity.
The commentary cites quarrelling as the cause of a group's weakened force; Jesus says a kingdom divided against itself is laid waste and a divided city or house will not stand.
The commentary says peace removes human estrangement; Jesus calls peacemakers blessed and children of God, assigning positive standing to the reconciling action.
The commentary's fractured bond must be repaired; Jesus instructs a worshiper to first reconcile with a brother who has a grievance, making restored relation prior to the offering.
The commentary makes truth something passed to the other person rather than fought over; Jesus tells one to confront a sinning brother privately with the aim of gaining him.
The commentary's haqq is shared within recovered affection; speaking truth in love builds growth into Christ, making the manner of transmission part of the truth's work.

column5: truth to neighbor because members of each other
column6: The commentary insists each participant gives and receives truth; Paul commands truthful speech to one's neighbor because believers are members of one another.

column5: patience bearing one another in love
column6: The commentary links patience to standing beside a companion; Paul joins patience, humility and bearing with one another in love as the practice of shared life.
The commentary's separated people are joined again; Paul asks believers to maintain the Spirit's unity in the bond of peace, turning attachment into a sustained task.
The commentary depicts enemies becoming close; Christ makes two groups one and breaks their dividing wall of hostility, an explicit transformation of social distance.
The commentary's sabr supports reconciliation where people have complaints; Paul tells believers to bear with and forgive one another when a complaint arises.
The commentary names affection and kinship as a bond whose absence marks distance; Paul calls love the bond that completes the virtues.
The commentary's repeated reciprocal verb makes each a giver and receiver of counsel; Paul says the word should dwell richly in the community as members teach and admonish one another.
The commentary highlights mutual exhortation as the way out of loss; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by deceitful sin.

column5: spur one another to love and good works
column6: The commentary joins mutual urging to righteous deeds and affection; Hebrews asks believers to consider how to stir each other toward love and good works.
The commentary's mutual action makes the community stronger; Paul tells believers to encourage and build one another, noting that they already do so.
The commentary's companion stands with others in patience; Paul assigns differentiated mutual duties to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with all.
The commentary's members give and receive aid; Paul tells them to bear each other's burdens, turning companionship into a concrete shared action.
The commentary cites both enemy-to-friend reversal and urging care for the poor; Paul commands feeding and giving drink to an enemy in need, locating the reversal in an act of mercy.
The commentary's enemies become friends through patiently choosing another response; Paul commands overcoming evil with good instead of being overcome by it.
The commentary invokes the failure to encourage food for the poor; John asks how God's love can remain in one who sees a needy brother and shuts up compassion.
The commentary's joined good deeds and shared haqq require action; John tells the community to love in deed and truth, not merely in speech.
The commentary joins righteous works to the ending of quarrel; James says a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by peacemakers.
The commentary begins with two sides contesting right; James asks where their wars and fights come from and locates them in desires at war within them.
The commentary moves from the lone human to a mutually sustaining believing group; Acts depicts the multitude of believers as one heart and soul, with no private claim to possessions.

column5: receive a slave as beloved brother
column6: The commentary's distant parties become family; Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother.
The commentary develops a specific transition from contention to togetherness; Paul appeals to Euodia and Syntyche by name to have the same mind in the Lord.
The commentary's close companion stands by members of the group; Paul asks a true companion to help the two women who worked beside him in the gospel.
The commentary says peace removes frightened separation; Peter withdraws from eating with Gentiles because he fears the circumcision group, a concrete reverse of shared company.
The commentary turns contest over haqq into truth shared for the community's good; Paul challenges Peter's withdrawal publicly because it contradicts the truth of the gospel.

The commentary treats peace as ending estrangement and drawing people into closeness; Hillel's maxim to be Aaron's disciple joins loving and pursuing peace with loving people and drawing them near Torah.
The commentary's two disputants need an action that reconnects them; this elaboration of Aaron as peacemaker depicts him approaching each estranged party to bring about reunion.

The commentary's rivals both assert right, yet peace changes the result; the rabbinic reading of judgment of peace in Zechariah 8:16 identifies compromise as a way to join adjudication and reconciliation.
The commentary's rival claims need the grievance to end so the bond can resume; Sirach commands forgiveness of a neighbor's wrong and connects that act with receiving pardon in prayer.
The commentary's reciprocal truth requires receiving as well as giving; the houses dispute law, but Hillel's house wins praise for humility and teaching Shammai's view before its own.

column5: make peace between those who quarrel
column6: The commentary moves from arguing parties to active reconciliation; the Didache forbids causing division and directs its reader to make peace among people in dispute.
The commentary repairs ties among believers; the Didache bars a person with a dispute from joining the assembly until reconciled, making peace a condition of its common offering.
The commentary's enemy becomes a close companion; after Jacob fears Esau, Esau runs to embrace and kiss him, giving a narrative instance of hostile distance becoming kinship.

column5: Joseph embraces and talks with brothers
column6: The commentary's separated kin are joined through interpersonal exchange; after revealing himself, Joseph kisses his brothers and they speak with him, reversing their earlier alienation.
The commentary's peace removes the fear that divided relatives; Joseph's brothers ask him to forgive their evil, and Joseph weeps when they speak, placing repaired kinship after wrongdoing.
The commentary's peace ends estrangement; this proverb contrasts covering an offense to seek love with repeating it and separating close friends.
The commentary makes mutual counsel an instrument of peace; this proverb opposes deceit in hearts that devise evil to joy among advisers who counsel peace.
The commentary's rival claims need a social practice short of estrangement; this proverb tells a person to argue his case with his neighbor directly and preserve another's confidence.
The commentary's close friend transmits helpful counsel; this proverb makes the sweetness of a friend come from earnest advice, giving content to affectionate exchange.

column5: truth and peace in priestly speech
column6: The commentary joins haqq to reconciliation; Malachi recalls true instruction in Levi's mouth and his walking with God in peace and uprightness, linking reliable teaching with peaceful conduct.
The commentary's right is to be practiced and shared, including care for the vulnerable; Isaiah demands learning good, seeking justice, correcting oppression and pleading for widow and orphan.
The commentary's two sides claiming right need a measure beyond assertion; Isaiah condemns those who justify the wicked for a bribe and deprive the righteous of right.
The commentary's remedy is mutual transmission of truth; Jeremiah depicts the inverse society, where people bend tongues for lies and do not advance by truth.
The commentary moves from estranged rivals to faithful companions; Jeremiah warns that every brother supplants and every neighbor slanders, a concrete collapse of the trusted bond.
The commentary makes peace an action that removes estrangement; this psalm commands turning from evil, doing good, and actively seeking and pursuing peace.
The commentary's haqq is shared toward peaceful belonging; this verse says those who love God's instruction have great peace and are not made to stumble by it.
The commentary values the tie of kinship after quarrel; this proverb likens an offended brother to a strong city and disputes to fortress bars, showing why reconciliation takes work.
The commentary's negative example is failure to urge feeding the needy; this command says to open one's hand to the poor and needy brother in the land.
The commentary condemns people who do not stir one another to feed the poor; this proverb says one who closes his ear to the poor person's cry will himself call and not be answered.

column5: speak for one who cannot speak
column6: The commentary turns haqq into an interpersonal duty; this verse directs the hearer to open his mouth for those unable to speak and for the rights of the destitute.
The commentary's rival claims require just dealing beyond self-interest; this verse asks the hearer to judge rightly and defend the poor and needy.
The commentary's communal peace requires a change from contention to good action; Isaiah links God's response to removing the yoke, threatening gesture and wicked speech from among the people.
The commentary points to failure to urge feeding the poor as a defect in shared life; Isaiah requires giving oneself to the hungry and satisfying the afflicted person's need.
The commentary contrasts the solitary human in loss with a mutually helpful company; Ecclesiastes says two are better than one because they gain a good return for their labor.
The commentary's companions give and receive aid; Ecclesiastes says one can lift the other when he falls, whereas the solitary person has no one to lift him.
The commentary says quarrelling dissipates a group's strength; Ecclesiastes says one person may be overpowered but two can stand against an attacker.
The commentary joins passed-on truth with affection; this proverb likens an honest answer to a kiss on the lips, making truthful response itself a sign of closeness.
The commentary says human bonds must be put right; Jesus makes the brother's grievance significant even at the altar, supplying the circumstance for the reconciliation commanded next.
The commentary's hostility is reversed toward intimacy; Jesus directs love and prayer toward enemies and persecutors, making the change an active response to opponents.
The commentary's togetherness must survive renewed wrongs; Peter asks how often to forgive a brother who sins against him, identifying a concrete strain on kinship.
The commentary's patience sustains restored ties; Jesus' answer to Peter rejects a small limit on forgiving a brother, extending reconciliation beyond a single settlement.
The commentary traces a move from frightened distance to enduring attachment; Paul suggests Onesimus was separated from Philemon for a time so Philemon might have him back forever.

column5: be at peace with one another
column6: The commentary ends with reciprocal action among believers; Jesus explicitly tells his disciples to have peace with one another after their dispute about rank.
The commentary's stranger or enemy can become a caring companion; the Samaritan responds with compassion to an injured traveler, crossing a socially fraught boundary.
The commentary cites mercy and the failure to encourage care for the needy; the Samaritan binds the traveler's wounds and takes him to shelter, embodying practical care.
The commentary moves from distance to close relation; Jesus' interlocutor identifies the neighbor as the one who showed mercy, making companionship an action rather than prior kinship.
The commentary's affectionate bond is maintained by sabr; Paul's description of love begins with patience and kindness, placing endurance inside interpersonal love.
The commentary binds love to mutual transmission of haqq; Paul says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth.
The commentary's companion stays with the community in patience; Paul's love bears and endures all things, giving that steadfastness a relational subject.

column5: members care for each other without division
column6: The commentary's reciprocal ethic overcomes separated parties; Paul's body image says members should have the same care for one another so the body has no division.
The commentary's one-sided isolation becomes shared life; Paul's members suffer or rejoice together as each member is affected.
The commentary says peace removes estrangement; Paul asks members to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another as God forgave them.
The commentary's hostile sides become a joined group; Paul describes reconciling both groups to God in one body through the cross and killing the hostility.
The commentary develops the close friend's affection and reciprocal giving; Paul commands brotherly love and outdoing one another in showing honor.
The commentary places responsibility on each party to end contention; Paul instructs believers, so far as it depends on them, to live peaceably with everyone.
The commentary's truth is passed without quarrel; James describes wisdom from above as peaceable, gentle and open to reason, an ethical mode for exchanging counsel.
The commentary cites quarrel as loss of collective strength; James says jealousy and selfish ambition bring disorder and every vile practice.

column5: turn a person wandering from truth
column6: The commentary's counsel is something believers do for one another; James envisages one member bringing back another who has wandered from the truth.
The commentary's mutual counsel averts loss; James says turning a sinner back from error saves that person's soul from death.
The commentary joins companions who might separate; Hebrews contrasts neglect of meeting together with mutual encouragement as the day approaches.
The commentary presents peace as an active repair of alienation; Hebrews commands pursuing peace with all, alongside holiness.
The commentary's link between people can be broken by a growing quarrel; Hebrews warns that a bitter root can spring up, cause trouble and defile many.
The commentary reverses rival claims into patient counsel; this instruction says the Lord's servant must not quarrel but be kind to everyone and able to teach.
The commentary's opening rivals fight over what they call right; this instruction says foolish and ignorant controversies produce quarrels, supplying a diagnosis of failed counsel.
The commentary's truth is conveyed to the other side instead of used for contention; the servant corrects opponents with gentleness in hope of their turning toward truth.
The commentary's reconciliation changes how people address one another; Titus orders believers to avoid quarrels and show gentleness to all people.
The commentary's separate claimants become an affectionate company; Paul asks the Philippians to be of one mind and the same love.
The commentary calls for righteous action joined to mutual counsel; Paul directs the community to do everything without grumbling or disputes.
The commentary develops closeness from estrangement; Peter asks all to have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love and humility.
The commentary's enemy-to-friend turn requires patience; Peter forbids returning evil or reviling in kind and commands blessing instead.
The commentary makes peace an action beyond ceasing a dispute; Peter tells readers to turn from evil, do good, and seek and pursue peace.

column5: love of brothers and escape from death
column6: The commentary contrasts the human in loss with believers joined by affection; John says love for brothers marks a passage from death to life.
The commentary insists on concrete closeness between believers; John calls one who claims to love God while hating a visible brother a liar.

column5: love of God entails love of brother
column6: The commentary binds faith to affection among companions; John says the command received from God is that the one loving God must also love his brother.
The commentary's members advise and sustain each other in affection; Jesus commands disciples to love one another as he has loved them.
The commentary's reciprocal bond defines the believing group; Jesus says others will recognize his disciples by their love for one another.
The commentary cites neglect of the needy as failure of shared obligation; Acts reports a complaint of Hellenists against Hebrews because their widows were overlooked in daily distribution.

The commentary moves contention toward companionship; Paul and Barnabas instead have a sharp disagreement and separate, showing that fellow believers' dispute can remain unresolved in the narrated moment.

The commentary initially places claim against claim, then makes truth serve the bond; this maxim distinguishes principled Hillel-Shammai disagreement from Korah's dispute, qualifying any simple condemnation of disagreement.
The commentary's parties can disagree yet preserve kinship; the houses of Shammai and Hillel did not refrain from marrying one another despite their disputes.

column5: Truth and Peace contest creating humanity
column6: The commentary's human being is threatened by contention while truth and peace must be joined; this midrash personifies Truth and Peace as disputing whether humanity should be created, because humans lie and quarrel.
The commentary binds haqq and sulh together; the rabbinic permission to change words for peace presses the question of how truthful speech serves a repaired relationship.
The commentary traces damage from disputes among believers; Clement asks why strife, anger, divisions and war appear among the community, confronting its internal fracture.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש (table sound correspondence)
column6: The source commentary calls the individual insan lost before mutual aid; this psalm asks what mortal enosh is that God remembers him. The proposed root link is phonetic, while the verse's frailty is a distinct sense.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's disputants each claim right while insan remains vulnerable; Job's speaker asks whether mortal enosh can be righteous before God. The proposed root correspondence illuminates mortal limitation, not the commentary's intimacy sense.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's human being is vulnerable apart from the group; Isaiah asks why one fears mortal enosh who will die like grass. The table's proposed root gives a frailty comparison rather than the commentary's sense of intimacy.

column5: ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's haqq is a shared right rather than a weapon of contention; Isaiah condemns those who decree unjust decrees using the proposed Hebrew root, showing that enacted rules can contradict right.

column5: ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח (table sound correspondence)
column6: The source commentary uses sulh for removing mutual estrangement; the psalm's royal rider advances for truth, humility and righteousness with a verb from Hebrew צלח. The martial advance differs from interpersonal peace, so the semantic link remains uncertain.

column5: ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary pairs salihat with faith and relational right; Jeremiah asks why the wicked's way prospers, using Hebrew צלח. This contrast shows that prospering in the corresponding root's Hebrew use does not itself establish righteous deeds.

column5: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
column6: The source commentary gives asr a secondary sense of affection or kinship; Joel calls a solemn assembly during communal crisis with a noun from Hebrew עצר. The gathering gives a social point of contact, but the roots' meanings may be unrelated.

column5: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's asr names a bond whose absence is felt; Isaiah says God cannot bear wrongdoing joined to a solemn assembly, using Hebrew עצר. An assembled group does not guarantee the just relation the commentary seeks.

column5: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary joins good action with communal attachment; God rejects Israel's festal assemblies in Amos, with Hebrew עצר, making mere gathering insufficient for the commentary's ethical togetherness.

column5: ص ل ح / Aramaic צלח (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's salihat are deeds performed by the believing group; Ezra's elders prosper as they build together under prophetic encouragement, using the proposed Aramaic root. Prosperous progress is a different sense from reconciliation.
The commentary begins with estrangement that peace must remove; Joseph's brothers hate him and cannot speak to him in peace, making the broken bond audible in their speech.

column5: comfort and kindly speech after fear
column6: The commentary's frightened separation becomes close companionship; Joseph tells his brothers not to fear, promises provision for their children, and speaks to their hearts after their plea for forgiveness.

The commentary answers the solitary human's loss through responsibility for companions; Cain evades responsibility for his murdered brother with this question, giving the stark opposite of mutual care.

The commentary moves from quarrels among kin to repaired ties; the list of hated acts ends with a false witness and a person who spreads strife among brothers, connecting untruth to broken fellowship.

column5: hatred stirs strife; love covers offenses
column6: The commentary reverses contention into affection; this proverb gives both movements in one line, with hatred stirring up disputes and love covering wrongs.
The commentary's close friend stands by a suffering group; this proverb says a friend loves at all times and a brother is born for adversity, joining affection to endurance.

The commentary's secondary senses include chosen intimacy and kinship; this proverb says a faithful friend may cling more closely than a brother, showing how a chosen bond can exceed inherited kinship.
The commentary asks that opposed people exchange good rather than contend over right; after Job's hard dispute with his friends, he prays for them and his fortunes are restored.
The commentary moves from contention to the truth and peace named later in Zechariah 8; this earlier verse recalls a time without peace, when every person was set against his neighbor.
The commentary's opening parties contest a right; Jesus urges agreement with an accuser while still on the way, providing a concrete settlement before judgment escalates the quarrel.
The commentary joins truthful counsel with repaired kinship; Jesus directs a disciple to rebuke a sinning brother and forgive him on repentance, giving both actions their place.
The commentary makes each believer responsible for another's progress; Paul calls them to pursue what makes for peace and builds one another up amid disputes over conduct.
The commentary stresses that each person both gives and receives counsel; Paul says the Romans are full of goodness and knowledge and able to admonish one another.
The commentary's claimed right can become injury to the other side; Paul says the litigating Corinthians themselves wrong and defraud their own brothers, reversing the ethic of mutual benefit.

column5: one hungry while another is full
column6: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the needy; in the Corinthians' common meal, one goes hungry while another becomes drunk, exposing a failed shared table.

column5: wait for one another at the meal
column6: The commentary's reciprocity must include material care; Paul tells the gathered Corinthians to wait for one another when they eat, answering the hungry member's exclusion in the same scene.
The commentary changes mutual action from dispute into affectionate service; Paul commands believers to use freedom to serve one another through love.
The commentary says contention weakens a community; Paul warns that biting and devouring one another can end with the disputants consumed by each other.
The commentary makes counsel a patient act for a companion's good; Paul directs spiritual members to restore someone caught in a transgression gently while watching their own vulnerability.
The commentary's separated people become a connected believing group; Paul says Christ's peace should rule in their hearts because they were called in one body.
The commentary's mutual action replaces retaliation; Paul forbids repaying evil for evil and directs believers always to seek good for one another and everyone.
The commentary transforms the opponent into a companion through counsel; Paul says the disobedient member is to be admonished as a brother rather than regarded as an enemy.

column5: brother or sister lacks food and clothes
column6: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the poor as a breach of mutual obligation; James places a needy brother or sister without daily food before the speaking community.

column5: go in peace without giving food
column6: The commentary insists on good deeds beside faith and on real care for the needy; James depicts someone wishing a needy person peace but withholding bodily necessities, exposing empty peaceful speech.

column5: confess and pray for one another
column6: The commentary's reciprocal counsel includes receiving help; James commands mutual confession and prayer so members may be healed, joining truthful disclosure to reciprocal care.
The commentary's patience permits estranged companions to stay together; Peter urges sustained love for one another because love covers a multitude of sins.
The commentary's close friendship issues in righteous action; John says Christ's laying down his life teaches believers to lay down their lives for brothers.
The commentary's peace removes fearful estrangement; Paul urges the community to forgive and comfort a punished person so excessive sorrow does not overwhelm him.
The commentary turns disagreement toward an enduring bond; Paul asks the community to confirm its love for the person it disciplined, making affection an explicit act of restoration.

The commentary's two sides can transmit truth and still become companions; this interpretation pictures father and son or teacher and pupil contending fiercely in Torah study yet parting as loving friends.

The commentary's reciprocal truth requires a giver and receiver; Rabbi Yohanan mourns Resh Lakish's challenging objections because their exchange developed the teaching, unlike a companion who only confirms him.
The commentary contrasts the human alone in loss with the belonging of companions; the Honi story ends with a scholar unable to find companions and a saying that one needs fellowship or death.

column5: if only for myself, what am I
column6: The commentary's solitary human cannot escape loss through self-concern; Hillel's question makes the inadequacy of living only for oneself explicit.
The commentary turns adversarial truth claims into mutual counsel; the Didache directs communal reproof without anger and in peace, joining correction to a nonhostile manner.

column5: share with a brother in need
column6: The commentary's fellowship reaches the needy rather than merely speaking to them; the Didache tells its reader to share possessions with a brother and not claim them as exclusively one's own.
The commentary names affection and kinship as bonds among close friends; Jonathan's soul is knit to David's and he loves David as himself, giving narrative form to chosen attachment.
The commentary's close companions remain connected through difficulty; Jonathan sends David away in peace under a covenant binding them and their descendants.

column5: loyal care due to a suffering friend
column6: The commentary's patient companion stands beside someone at risk of loss; Job complains that a suffering person should receive steadfast kindness from a friend rather than abandonment.
The commentary's lost affection leaves a human isolated; Job laments that intimate friends abhor him and those he loved have turned against him, an inverse of patient companionship.
The commentary's isolated sufferer is rejoined by people who stand with him; Job's brothers, sisters and former acquaintances eat with him and comfort him after his ordeal.
The commentary's sabr allows enmity to become intimacy; this proverb calls slowness to anger prudent and overlooking an offense a person's glory.
The commentary's secondary asr sense names affection and kinship by their absence; this proverb warns against forsaking one's friend or father's friend when trouble comes.
The commentary's reconciliation reverses fear and withdrawal; Micah says not to trust a neighbor or intimate friend, depicting social breakdown at the level of close ties.

column5: no longer teach neighbor and brother to know God
column6: The commentary gives believers a continuing duty to urge one another in truth; Jeremiah imagines a new covenant in which neighbor and brother no longer teach each other to know God because all know him, a particular limit on mutual instruction.
The commentary's close friend gives security after frightened separation; Sirach calls a faithful friend a sturdy shelter and a treasure, making companionship protective.
The commentary's peace must heal the bond beneath formal settlement; Jesus closes the unforgiving servant story by requiring forgiveness of one's brother from the heart.
The commentary's reciprocal action draws separated members into concord; Jesus says two who agree on earth about a request will be heard by the Father, within his teaching on community disputes.
The commentary's intimate friend receives truth rather than being held at a distance; Jesus calls disciples friends because he has made known to them what he heard from his Father.
The commentary's estranged parties become companions; Paul commands mutual welcome as Christ has welcomed them, giving the bond a concrete reception practice.

column5: speech that builds the other up
column6: The commentary's mutual exhortation gives another person what is needed; Paul asks for speech suited to building up hearers and giving them grace, rather than harmful talk.
The commentary starts with rival claims inside a group; Paul points to jealousy and strife among the Corinthians as evidence of immature, merely human behavior.
The commentary's failed urging to feed the poor has communal consequences; Paul rebukes the Corinthians for shaming members who have nothing at their shared meal.
The commentary's reciprocal care keeps others close; Peter asks members to show hospitality to one another without complaint, giving affectionate attachment a household practice.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel requires receiving the other's word and patient speech; James commands quick hearing, slow speaking and slow anger.

column5: warn then separate from divisive person
column6: The commentary emphasizes holding a group together through counsel; Titus directs warning a divisive person twice and then having nothing further to do with him, marking a limit to maintained companionship.
The commentary contrasts the solitary human with a believing company; Hillel's instruction not to separate oneself from the community treats continued belonging as a deliberate duty.
The commentary treats reconciliation as work among opposed people; the rabbinic list of deeds whose benefits extend into the world to come includes making peace between one person and another.

column5: correct rather than hate a person
column6: The commentary's counsel must be joined to affection; the Didache forbids hatred and distinguishes those one should correct, pray for, or love beyond oneself.

column5: ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's haqq is a claim that must serve right relations; Wisdom says rulers decree what is just, using Hebrew חקק. The proposed consonantal correspondence links right to a public decree, though the Hebrew root's meaning is legal enactment.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary's insan is vulnerable to loss; the psalm says God returns mortal enosh to dust. The table proposes the root correspondence, while the psalm's concern is mortality rather than intimacy.

column5: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש (table sound correspondence)
column6: The commentary begins with the human in loss; Daniel's vision presents a human-like figure coming with heaven's clouds, an exalted use of Aramaic enash. The roots may correspond, but the figure is not the commentary's ordinary solitary person.

column5: peaceful speech to someone who sinned
column6: The commentary's counsel repairs a bond after wrongdoing; this testament urges love among brothers and peaceful speech to someone who sins against a companion. The exact verse division within chapter 6 is uncertain from memory.
